segments.title: Intercepting Graf Spee without entering neutral waters
segments.body: On 16 December 1939, Harwood has three cruisers to cover Graf Spee's possible departures from Montevideo. A move toward Argentina would complicate interception. Another possible route risks bringing the fighting within the three-mile territorial limit, where the ships are not supposed to fight. The direction of Graf Spee's departure therefore affects both Harwood's deployment and the risk of fighting in neutral waters.

evidence.note: The discussion considers movement toward Argentina, other possible departure directions, the risk of fighting within the three-mile limit, and coverage by only three cruisers. Exact map directions and garbled place names are not reconstructed.

segments.summary: Harwood must cover Graf Spee's possible routes with three cruisers while avoiding a battle in neutral waters inside the three-mile territorial limit.

segments.title: British surveillance tracks any move by Graf Spee
segments.body: Harwood receives continuous updates on Graf Spee from an American radio contact. Merchant ships in the harbor offer another way to report her movements: the fine for transmitting there is only £5, which Britain would likely repay and might supplement with a reward. Ambassador Millington-Drake, MI6 officers, and the naval attache add observers ashore. Langsdorff realizes that Harwood will learn of any move. Harwood might also have an aircraft airborne, making even a night departure difficult to hide.

evidence.note: Harwood receives continuous reports from an American radio contact. Merchant ships can transmit for a five-pound fine, British officials and intelligence officers watch Graf Spee, and an aircraft may also be airborne.

segments.summary: Radio reports, merchant ships, and observers ashore make even a night departure by Admiral Graf Spee difficult to conceal from Harwood.

segments.title: Langsdorff prepares for Uruguay's deadline
segments.body: Langsdorff's options narrow as Graf Spee's permitted stay approaches its end. He will neither surrender nor sacrifice roughly a thousand sailors in a hopeless action, because he believes a thousand living heroes are better than a thousand dead ones. He continues to seek more time while preparing on the assumption that Uruguay will refuse it. A German vessel sits between Graf Spee and the shore as cover, while German-owned tugs from Argentina move closer and begin transferring people and stores. Those preparations show that his plan for the next day is already under way.

evidence.note: As the 72-hour deadline approached, Langsdorff refused to sacrifice his crew. A German vessel screened Graf Spee from the shore while German-owned tugs from Argentina transferred people and stores for his chosen plan.

segments.summary: With the 72-hour limit expiring the next day, Langsdorff refuses to surrender or sacrifice his crew and starts moving people and stores for the plan he has chosen.

segments.title: Four frantic days cannot restore Graf Spee
segments.body: The wider South Atlantic campaign contains long stretches of sailing and waiting, followed by the sudden tempo of the Battle of the River Plate and the Montevideo crisis. Graf Spee spends three days in port, and the fourth will bring the episode to its conclusion. Repairs restore part of the ship's capability, but never enough for her to fight her way out. Diplomatic and logistical work continues at speed even though it cannot change the basic military position. A slow commerce-raiding campaign has become a crisis governed by port deadlines and approaching enemy forces.

evidence.note: Four frantic days at the River Plate followed the wider campaign's long periods of sailing and waiting, but repairs could not restore Graf Spee enough for her to fight her way out.

segments.summary: Four frantic days in Montevideo follow the South Atlantic campaign's long periods of waiting, with repairs still insufficient for Graf Spee to fight her way out.

segments.title: Battle may have worsened Graf Spee's machinery wear
segments.body: Some reports attribute Graf Spee's engine and piston problems to battle damage, while others suggest that long service without maintenance caused at least part of the trouble. The evidence in this account does not settle the issue. Royal Navy reports on heavily used ships offer a broader comparison: machinery worn by long operations often develops worse problems after combat. That possibility matters when judging why Graf Spee could not regain full fighting condition in Montevideo. Operational endurance also depends on whether a ship has had time to service its machinery.

evidence.note: Reports disagree over whether Graf Spee's engine and piston trouble came from battle damage or extended use without servicing; combat may have worsened existing machinery wear.

segments.summary: Reports of engine trouble suggest that combat may have worsened machinery wear caused by prolonged operations without servicing.

segments.title: Ajax and Achilles refuel while ammunition runs short
segments.body: Ajax and Achilles refuel from a Royal Fleet Auxiliary vessel on 16 December. Cumberland still has plenty of fuel aboard. Ammunition is a separate constraint: Ajax and Achilles are short of it, while Cumberland has plenty. These differences in supplies affect the readiness of Harwood's cruisers for a possible departure by Graf Spee.

evidence.note: Ajax and Achilles oil from an RFA. Cumberland still has ample fuel, and the ammunition shortage in the other cruisers contrasts with Cumberland's plentiful supply.

segments.summary: Ajax and Achilles take on fuel from a Royal Fleet Auxiliary vessel, but their ammunition remains scarce compared with Cumberland's.

segments.title: Ark Royal approaches the River Plate at more than 30 knots
segments.body: Renown and Ark Royal are approaching at full speed, with a stop in Brazil expected the next day. Ark Royal is making more than 30 knots. Several of her engineering chief petty officers later claimed that this was the fastest she ever sailed. Her captain had demanded every knot the machinery could deliver. The approach adds urgency to British preparations for Graf Spee's possible departure.

evidence.note: Renown and Ark Royal approach at full speed and expect a Brazilian stop the next day. Ark Royal exceeds 30 knots, and engineering chief petty officers later claim it was her fastest passage, following the captain's demand for every possible knot.

segments.summary: Renown and Ark Royal hurry toward the River Plate, with engineering personnel later claiming that Ark Royal never sailed faster.
